name: Pocket watch

card.summary: A chained timepiece carried in a waistcoat or trouser pocket that works as a vintage, formal style accessory.

quick.overview:
A pocket watch is a small watch carried in a pocket and usually secured with a chain or fob. For appearance it works as a classic accessory: worn with a waistcoat or three-piece suit, the chain across the vest adds a vintage, polished look.

Pocket watches were the most common kind of watch from the 16th century until wristwatches took over after World War I. Today they are mainly a fashion item and a collector's piece, with antique and quartz versions both available.
quick.how: The watch sits in a waistcoat or trouser pocket, with the chain attached to a waistcoat button, lapel or belt loop. Decorative fobs and small charms can hang from the chain. It is typically paired with formal or vintage-style outfits such as three-piece suits.
quick.risks: Antique movements are delicate and may need professional servicing. A chain can snag on clothing, and the watch can be damaged if dropped. Cases and chains vary widely in quality and metal.

lead: A pocket watch is a timepiece designed to be carried in a pocket rather than strapped to the wrist, and it was the most common type of watch from the 16th century until wristwatches became popular after World War I [1]. A chain or fob secures it to a waistcoat, lapel or belt loop so it is not dropped [1].

For someone working on their style, a pocket watch is a formal accessory. Worn with a waistcoat, the chain and fob add a vintage, tailored detail, and decorative fobs can be hung from the chain [1]. Interest has been sustained by the steampunk movement and a late-1970s and early-1980s revival of three-piece suits [1].
Modern pocket watches are mainly worn as fashion accessories, and quartz versions exist alongside mechanical antiques [1].

angle.text: The chain and watch case are visible accessories that complete a waistcoat or three-piece outfit. People use them to add a classic, put-together detail to formal clothing.

paras: Pocket watches consist of a metal case, crystal, dial and movement, with a bow that attaches to a chain or fob [2]. Common styles are the open-face with an exposed dial, the hunter with a snap-shut cover and the demi-hunter with a small viewing window in the lid [2]. They are generally larger than wristwatches, around 40 to 60 mm in diameter [2].

The earliest wearable timepieces were 16th-century European clock-watches, large drum-shaped brass cases worn on chains around the neck, which became rounder and flatter so they could be pocketed [1]. Men began carrying them in pockets in the 17th century, a change traditionally linked to the introduction of waistcoats, and glass faces appeared around 1610 [1]. Railways spread their use in the late 19th century and led to strict timekeeping standards in 1893 [1]. Wristwatches and later smartphones displaced them, though they remain in use in Japanese railway work and as retirement gifts in the US [1].

Chains secure the watch to clothing, and shorter straps or fobs were used where a long chain was impractical [1]. Chains often carried decorative pendants bearing club or society emblems, and practical items such as winding keys and cigar cutters [1]. Women's watches typically stayed pendant-style with more decorative fobs [1].

timeline.event: European clock-watches worn on chains around the neck appear [1].
Men begin carrying watches in waistcoat pockets [1].
Wristwatches overtake pocket watches in popularity [1].
